meta.title: Who really said "The cure for boredom is curiosity. There is no cure for curiosity"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Dorothy Parker — she died in 1967 and the line first appears in 1980, credited to Ellen Parr. QI traces the swap to two adjacent entries in an alphabetical list.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The cure for boredom is curiosity. There is no cure for curiosity'?
meta.ogDescription: Ellen Parr, in Reader’s Digest, December 1980 — thirteen years after Dorothy Parker’s death. Parr and Parker sat next to each other in an alphabetical list.

answer.label: Not Dorothy Parker — actually Ellen Parr
answer.authorDates: Dates unknown — no biographical details have been located
answer.sourceLine: The earliest known appearance is Reader’s Digest for December 1980, in the “Quotable Quotes” column, where the words are credited to Ellen Parr. Dorothy Parker had been dead for thirteen years. Quote Investigator’s conclusion is that the saying “should be credited to Ellen Parr” — while noting that it has been unable to find any biographical details about her at all.
answer.confidenceText: Disputed as to Parker, who is excluded on dates. Ellen Parr holds the earliest credit, but almost nothing is known about her.

source.heading: The earliest documented appearance
source.excerpt: The cure for boredom is curiosity. There is no cure for curiosity. —Ellen Parr
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ gives the earliest instance as Reader’s Digest, December 1980, in a column called “Quotable Quotes,” where the words are ascribed to Ellen Parr. A Centre Daily Times item of March 1981 and a 1984 Alaskan newspaper cryptogram both still credit Parr.
Dorothy Parker died on 7 June 1967 ↗, thirteen years before that first printing. QI states there is “no substantive evidence that she employed this saying.”

QI identifies a specific mechanism for the swap: a March 1996 mailing-list digest listed quotations alphabetically by surname, placing a Parker item (“The two most beautiful words in the English language are: ‘Cheque enclosed.’”) immediately above the Parr item. QI hypothesises ↗ that an inattentive reader merged the two. The first reassignment to Parker that QI records is an April 1997 Usenet post.

The Parker guess felt plausible because curiosity really is one of her subjects: her 1926 collection Enough Rope contains the poem “Inventory,” whose second couplet reads “Four be the things I’d been better without: / Love, curiosity, freckles, and doubt.” We confirmed that text in the full Project Gutenberg edition ↗. Sounding like an author is not evidence of authorship.
source.excerptNote: As printed in the December 1980 “Quotable Quotes” column and reproduced by Quote Investigator ↗. We were not able to consult a copy of the issue itself.
source.rightsHolder: Ellen Parr or her estate; first published in Reader’s Digest, December 1980
source.rightsNote: First published in December 1980 — far too recent for the United States public domain, which currently reaches published works through 1930. Rights would rest with Ellen Parr or her estate, and possibly with the magazine; because no biographical trace of Parr has been found, the holder cannot be identified with confidence. Parker’s own 1926 Enough Rope, quoted above for contrast, is public domain.

author.name: Ellen Parr
author.heading: About Ellen Parr
author.metaLine: Dates unknown · credited in Reader’s Digest, December 1980
author.bio: Almost nothing is known about Ellen Parr. Quote Investigator, which traced this saying through eight decades of print, states plainly that it “has not located any biographical details for Parr.” She survives in the record as a name at the end of one sentence in a December 1980 magazine column — and as the person that sentence was subsequently taken from.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: A staple of graduation speeches and social media, almost always over Dorothy Parker’s name. The dates rule her out.

items.why: Parker died in June 1967; the saying is not documented anywhere until December 1980. QI ↗ finds “no substantive evidence that she employed this saying,” and dates the first Parker credit it can locate to an April 1997 Usenet post.

In a March 1996 mailing-list digest of quotations sorted by surname, a Parker line sat directly above the Parr line. QI hypothesises ↗ that a careless scan of those two adjacent entries produced the misattribution — “Parr” and “Parker” being alphabetically almost identical.
“There is no cure for curiosity” had been circulating on its own for decades: QI ↗ prints an instance from the Boston Sunday Post in 1915, which continues “It must be outgrown or endured.”

misattribution.truthLine: The credit belongs to Ellen Parr, about whom even Quote Investigator ↗ has been unable to learn anything — a reminder that the real author of a famous line is often nobody famous at all.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: This is the clearest documented case of a misattribution with a known mechanism. Most fake quotes simply drift; this one can be traced to a specific bad habit — reading a list sorted by surname and picking up the wrong neighbour. “Parr” and “Parker” sit within two letters of each other, and in the 1996 digest QI reproduces, the two entries are one line apart.
The cost is borne by Ellen Parr, whose only known trace in the historical record is this sentence, and who has now largely lost it to a more famous name.
context.pull: One line apart in an alphabetical list, and the credit moved for good.

sourcesVerified.claim: QI gives the earliest instance as Reader's Digest, December 1980, "Quotable Quotes", ascribed to Ellen Parr, and concludes the statement "should be credited to Ellen Parr".
QI states Dorothy Parker died in 1967 and there is "no substantive evidence that she employed this saying"; it has "not located any biographical details for Parr".

QI reproduces a March 1996 alphabetical mailing-list digest in which a Dorothy Parker item sits immediately above the Ellen Parr item, and hypothesises this adjacency caused the misattribution; the first Parker ascription it records is an April 1997 Usenet post.
QI prints an 1915 Boston Sunday Post instance of "There is no cure for curiosity. It must be outgrown or endured."

Project Gutenberg's full text of Enough Rope (1926) contains the poem "Inventory" with the lines "Four be the things I'd been better without: / Love, curiosity, freckles, and doubt." — verified against the ebook text.
A scanned 1926 printing of Dorothy Parker's Enough Rope is catalogued by the Internet Archive.
Wikiquote gives Dorothy Parker's dates as 22 August 1893 to 7 June 1967, and its Misattributed section does not list this saying.
Reader's Digest is an American general-interest magazine.
